 Live .  5,939 viewing 5939 viewing Live page Updated 1 minute ago UK inflation hits highest rate in a year, driven by rising fuel prices
 Summary
 The UK inflation rate rose again in October, hitting 3.6% 
 It's the fourth consecutive monthly rise, and the highest rate in a year - the Bank of England's target is 2%
 The Office for National Statistics says higher fuel bills were "once again a major contributor" - but other things also increased in price, including computer software and cat food 
 The government says wars in the Middle East and Ukraine have "pushed up costs around the world" 
 But the shadow chancellor says the government's decision to "hike taxes and employment costs" have contributed to the inflation increase 
 Most economists expected a rise in October - and more increases are expected 
 Earlier this month, the Bank raised interest rates to 4% - the first increase since 2023 - in an effort to curb inflation
 Live Reporting
 Edited by Tinshui Yeung, with cost of living correspondent Kevin Peachey
 Forecast predicts 26% rise in energy prices in January published at 08:07 GMT 08:07 GMT Breaking 
 Kevin Peachey 
Cost of living correspondent 
 We've just had the latest forecast on the level of domestic energy prices in January, and it is an eye-watering 26% rise.
 Energy consultancy Cornwall Insight, which has a good track record with its predictions, says that the forecast rise would take domestic dual-fuel bills to their highest level since 2023.
 Millions of homes in England, Scotland and Wales are on tariffs affected by regulator Ofgem's price cap, set every three months. The next change for January will be officially announced next Wednesday.
 Cornwall Insight's forecast suggests that a household using a typical amount of gas and electricity will pay £2,166 a year, an increase of £443 from current levels over the course of a year. 
 The government has promised a £100 payment for people living in homes in council tax bands A to D to help cover winter energy costs.

 Inflation rates are lower in some areas, such as hotel stays published at 07:53 GMT 07:53 GMT 
 Dharshini David 
Deputy economics editor 
 Image source, The Washington Post via Getty Images Few surprises in the nudge up in the overall inflation rate last month, as higher global energy costs propelled an increase in domestic gas bills - and the price of road fuels.
 But tucked away in the detail, encouraging news too. Inflation in areas such as hotel stays and cafe meals slowed. And food inflation, at less than 1%, was at its lowest for five years. 
 Not only do such items help keep a lid on overall inflation - but also suggest that higher energy bills are not fuelling higher prices in some other items. Earlier in the month, the Bank of England also noted that some firms appeared to be absorbing such cost increases rather than passing them on. 
 Of course that could change in coming months, and analysts do expect inflation to tick up a bit more as the higher energy costs of the last couple months keep domestic heating bills high. 
 But much depends on the path of events in the Middle East, and the impact they have on global energy costs.

 What is driving the inflation rate higher? published at 07:43 GMT 07:43 GMT 
 Kevin Peachey 
Cost of living correspondent 
 Image source, Universal Images Group via Getty Images There are some obvious and some surprising drivers of the increasing rate of price rises.
 The impact of higher diesel costs was blindingly obvious for motorists and anyone passing a petrol station.
 A rise in tobacco duty took effect on 1 October, which was earlier than the previous year, so that's had an upward effect.
 Some of the other, somewhat smaller, moves up included the prices of action cameras, water sports equipment, cat food, computer software and non-fiction paperbacks.

 Middle East conflict and Russia-Ukraine war push up costs 'around the world' - Treasury published at 07:33 GMT 07:33 GMT 
 Image source, PA Media Image caption, (Left to right) Financial Secretary to the Treasury James Murray, Chancellor John Healey and Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds
 In a statement responding to the rise in the inflation rate, Chief Secretary to the Treasury Emma Reynolds says the conflict in the Middle East and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have pushed up costs around the world.
 "The Household Energy Payment, announced in our Budget, is providing £100 directly into 20 million bank accounts in January which will help to give families breathing space now," she says.
 "The Budget also started the long-term action needed to get energy costs down for good, including an end to levies on household bills, scrapping standing charges and ensuring Britain is better protected from global shocks in the future."

 Shadow chancellor blames inflation rise on energy costs and Labour taxes published at 07:19 GMT 07:19 GMT 
 Image source, PA Media The shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, blames the fourth successive rise in the inflation rate on the UK’s "soaring energy costs" and Labour’s decision to "hike taxes and employment costs".
 "They didn’t have to do that. But now we will all pay the price," he says in a post on social media.
 In a separate statement, he says: "Higher inflation means the pound in everyone’s pocket is worth less. Families with a mortgage now face the prospect of higher interest rates for longer."

 First impact of October energy price cap rise published at 07:10 GMT 07:10 GMT 
 Kevin Peachey 
Cost of living correspondent 
 Image source, PA Media These inflation figures are the first to be impacted by the near 4% rise in domestic energy prices in October.
 A household in England, Scotland and Wales using a typical amount of gas and electricity is paying £60 a year more than previously, assuming they are not on a fixed tariff.
 The price cap, set by regulator Ofgem, changes every three months and forecasts suggest a big rise is coming in January.

 Fuel prices 'once again' a major contributor, says ONS published at 07:07 GMT 07:07 GMT 
 Following the announcement, ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner says fuel prices are "once again a major contributor" to the increase in the annual rate.
 He says: "Annual costs of both raw materials and goods leaving factories continue to climb, driven by higher crude oil and petrol prices, respectively."

 Rising inflation rate isn't over yet published at 07:04 GMT 07:04 GMT 
 Kevin Peachey 
Cost of living correspondent 
 Image source, PA Media The 3.6% rate of inflation in October is bang in line with analysts' expectations.
 It is also in line with the experiences of consumers, with motor fuel costs key to the rising cost of living .
 That's the fourth consecutive rise in the rate of inflation.
 Economists and the public believe there is more to come, with October's figure part of a trend that is expected to see price rises of essential goods and services accelerate.

 Inflation rate rises to 3.6% published at 07:01 GMT 07:01 GMT Breaking 
 The rate of inflation rose to 3.6% in the year to October, according to the latest figures just released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS).
 This follows the rise from 3.1% to 3.5% in the year to September, and marks the fourth successive increase.
 We'll bring you more in our next post.

 What is inflation and why has it been rising? published at 06:55 GMT 06:55 GMT 
 Inflation is the increase in the price of something over time.
 For example, if a chocolate bar costs £1 but rises to £1.10 a year later, annual chocolate inflation is 10%.
 If it had risen to £1.05 instead, the inflation rate would be lower, at 5%. That would still be an increase, but a smaller one.
 When we say the inflation rate has fallen, it often means prices are still rising, just not as quickly.
 Image source, Getty Images The Office for National Statistics (ONS) tracks the prices of hundreds of everyday items and services, including food and fuel, to produce the Consumer Prices Index (CPI). The latest figure is published monthly.
 Recent rises in inflation have largely been driven by higher fuel prices, which have increased since the outbreak of the war in Iran.
 After the US and Israel attacked Iran in February, Iran threatened shipping travelling through the Strait of Hormuz, driving up oil transport costs, including maritime insurance.

 Fuel and energy are key to inflation rate published at 06:49 GMT 06:49 GMT 
 Kevin Peachey 
Cost of living correspondent 
 Analysts are expecting the inflation rate to keep rising into next year. The Bank of England thinks it is heading to just under 5% next spring.
 The big driver of those increases is motor fuel and domestic energy costs.
 Drivers have already been grappling with higher prices at the pump. Many have limited the amount they spend each time, rather than filling the tank. In recent days, those prices have come down a little.
 Domestic energy prices went up in October, but the big household energy price spike is coming in January. Exactly how big, we will find out for certain next week, but forecasts have suggested it will be enough to have a notable impact on the overall inflation rate in the new year.

 Bank of England expects inflation to keep rising published at 06:40 GMT 06:40 GMT 
 The release of today's figures comes a fortnight after the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years.
 On 5 November, the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee increased rates from 3.75% to 4% in a bid to curb inflation, driven mainly by the conflict's impact on global oil prices.
 The Bank uses interest rates to slow inflation, which it now expects to peak at 4.9% in the middle of next year. It doesn't expect inflation to return to its 2% target until 2028.
 In an "adverse scenario", where the US-Iran war escalates further and sends oil prices higher, inflation could reach 6.2% in 2027, the Bank suggested.

 Latest inflation figures to be released soon published at 06:27 GMT 06:27 GMT 
 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, A rise in fuel prices - driven by the war in Iran - has contributed to the increasing rate of inflation
 The latest inflation figures are due to be released at 07:00 GMT , with forecasts suggesting official data will show prices have continued to rise.
 Economists at the Bank of England and the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) have forecast inflation will increase , external into next year.
 In the year to September, inflation hit 3.5% - the highest figure since October 2025. Those figures, released last month, were up from 3.1% in the year to August. That is higher than the Bank of England’s target of 2%.
 If today's figures show the rate has risen again, it will be the fourth successive increase, and the first since Chancellor John Healey's "breathing space" Budget was delivered on 28 October.
 Stay with us as we bring you the figure as soon as it's announced, as well as what it means for you.
